To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the self-assembly properties of DNA-binding proteins are profoundly altered by their ability to switch between an on (binding) and off (nonbinding) conformation.

(1) the self-assembly properties of chromatin-associating proteins are strongly affected by their ability to switch between on and off states, and (2) the resulting clusters are dynamic and have properties consistent with those of nuclear bodies.
(1) protein switching leads to the formation and maintenance of clusters of self-limited size, and (2) protein switching reshapes chromatin contacts, favoring short-range contacts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the biophysical mechanisms that shape the structure of the genome and its associated proteins.
the formation and properties of chromatin domains and nuclear bodies in the cell nucleus.
understanding the physical mechanisms that govern the formation of nuclear bodies and topologically associating chromatin domains.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
posttranslational modifications of chromatin-bridge proteins can be a generic mechanism for the self-assembly and dynamics of nuclear bodies.
the protein switching mechanism is a generic and effective mechanism to form nuclear bodies, and it can be extended to other biological systems.
the protein switching mechanism, which is a generic feature of the DNA binding protein dynamics, is able to explain a wide range of experimental observations on nuclear bodies and chromatin domains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dynamic nature of chromatin is a consequence of the fact that chromatin-bridges are not permanent, but are rather constantly formed and disassembled.
protein switching is a mechanism to generate highly dynamic protein clusters with the characteristics of membrane-free nuclear bodies.
posttranslational modifications of chromatin-binding proteins are a general mechanism for generating highly dynamic, nonequilbrium, protein clusters with nuclear body-like properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
protein switching, a ubiquitous feature of chromatin-binding proteins, can drive the formation of nuclear bodies and chromatin domains.
the formation of nuclear bodies and chromatin domains is a dynamic, nonequilibriums process that is driven by the ability of the proteins to switch between bound and unbound states.
the properties of chromatin domains are shaped not only by the intrinsic binding properties of the proteins that bridge DNA, but also by the kinetics of their binding.
